astro-01.title: Looking at the Sky
explain: When you look up at the night sky, the stars seem to be attached to a huge dome surrounding us. Astronomy uses this appearance as a model: we imagine the sky as the inner surface of a giant sphere centered on us. This is called the **celestial sphere**. In reality, the stars are not all attached to one surface, and their distances differ. The celestial sphere is a convenient **model** for describing the positions of stars.

To state a position in the sky, two values are needed.
- **Azimuth**: the direction measured along the horizon. It is stated as north, east, south or west, or as an angle measured clockwise from north, taken as 0 degrees.
- **Altitude**: the angle measured upward from the horizon. The horizon is 0 degrees, and the point directly overhead is 90 degrees.

explain.alt: On the left is a circular compass diagram with N at the top, S at the bottom, E on the right and W on the left. From the center, a line extends between north and east, ending in an orange dot, and an arc from north to that line is labeled azimuth. On the right are a horizontal line (the horizon) and a line rising obliquely above it; the angle between the two lines is labeled altitude, and a star sits at the end of the rising line.

explain: Over the course of a day, the Sun, the Moon and the stars generally rise in the east, pass through the southern sky and set in the west. It looks as if the sky is turning around us, but in reality it is **Earth** that we stand on that moves. Earth undergoes **rotation** from west to east. Rotation is the motion of Earth about its own axis, and one turn takes about a day. It is the same illusion as the scenery outside a moving train appearing to flow backward. Motion that arises from Earth's motion in this way is called **apparent motion**.

In the Northern Hemisphere, when you look at the northern sky, the **North Star** stays in nearly the same place while the other stars circle around it. This is because the North Star lies close to the northward extension of Earth's rotation axis.

The stars of the night sky have long been grouped and given names. A named group of this kind is a **constellation**. Today the International Astronomical Union divides the whole sky into 88 constellation regions. A constellation is therefore both a **region** of the sky and a **name**. Stars belonging to the same constellation are not necessarily close to one another. They only appear in similar directions in the sky, and their distances from us can differ greatly.

examples.title: How far does a star move in one hour?
body: Earth rotates about 360 degrees in about one day, so in one hour it turns through 360 ÷ 24 = 15 degrees. If you take a long-exposure photograph of the night sky, the stars leave arc-shaped trails; over two hours, a star traces an arc of about 30 degrees.
From how much the stars appear to move, we can estimate how fast Earth rotates.

astro-02.title: The Solar System
explain: The **Solar System** consists of the Sun and the celestial bodies that are bound to it by its gravity and orbit around it. The Sun is a **star** that emits its own light, and it contains most of the mass of the Solar System. There are eight **planets** that orbit the Sun. Since 2006, Pluto has been classified not as a planet but as a **dwarf planet**.
In order of distance from the Sun, the planets are **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. Memorizing this order will make the explanations that follow easier.

Planets are divided into two broad groups.
- **Terrestrial planets**: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They are relatively small and have solid rocky surfaces.
- **Giant planets**: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They are much larger, and their surfaces are not clearly solid. Jupiter and Saturn are mainly gas, while Uranus and Neptune are known to contain much ice.

A body that orbits a planet is called a **satellite**. Earth's Moon is a satellite of Earth. The Moon does not emit its own light, but it shines brightly by **reflecting sunlight**. The Moon takes about a month to orbit Earth, and half of its round body is always lit by the Sun. However, as seen from Earth, the angle between the Moon and the Sun changes, so how much of the sunlit side faces us also changes. This is the **phase change of the Moon**.

astro-03.title: Earth's Motion and the Seasons
explain:
Earth moves in two ways.
- **Rotation**: motion about its axis. It completes about one turn per day, which produces day and night.
- **Revolution**: motion around the Sun. It completes one turn in about a year.

Earth's rotation axis does not stand upright relative to its orbital path; it is **tilted** by about 23.5 degrees. More importantly, the direction of this tilt stays nearly unchanged throughout the year. Wherever Earth is in its orbit, the north end of its rotation axis points in the same direction in space.

explain.alt: In the center is the orange Sun, and at four points along the elliptical orbit around it are Earths. The left one is (A), the top one is (B), the right one is (C) and the bottom one is (D). Every Earth's axis is tilted to the right by the same amount, and the upper end of each axis has an orange dot. The left Earth's upper end is tilted toward the Sun, which is on its right, while the right Earth's upper end is tilted away from the Sun, which is on its left. The top and bottom Earths have their axes tilted sideways. A label at the lower left says the orange dot marks the north end of the rotation axis.
explain.caption: Earth at four points on its orbit (schematic, not to scale)

explain: In the position on the left, Earth's north end is tilted toward the Sun. The Northern Hemisphere then receives sunlight more directly and for longer. Days are long and the midday Sun is high, so the same area receives more heat. This is **summer** in the Northern Hemisphere. At the opposite position, the north end is tilted away from the Sun, so the days are short and the Sun is low, and it is **winter**. The top and bottom positions in the figure are when spring and autumn occur, and day and night are nearly equal in length.
The Southern Hemisphere is the opposite. When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, the Southern Hemisphere has winter.

A common misconception is that **summer comes because Earth gets closer to the Sun**. This is not true. Earth's orbit is nearly circular, so its distance from the Sun differs by only a few percent, and Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. Also, when the Northern Hemisphere has summer, the Southern Hemisphere has winter; if distance were the cause, both hemispheres would share the same season. The cause of the seasons is not distance but the **axial tilt** of Earth.

examples.title: If there were no tilt
body: Suppose Earth's rotation axis were not tilted relative to its orbit but stood upright. Then the angle at which sunlight reaches the ground and the length of the day would be nearly the same all year round, everywhere on Earth. There would be no clear seasonal change like the one we have now. This thought experiment confirms that the seasons come from the tilt, not from distance.

astro-04.title: Stars
explain: A **star** is a huge ball of gas that emits its own light. In the core of a star, light nuclei fuse together in a process called nuclear fusion, which produces enormous amounts of energy. The Sun is also a star. It looks large and bright only because it is the nearest star to Earth. Planets and the Moon do not emit their own light.

Two things must be distinguished when talking about how bright a star is.
- **Apparent brightness**: the brightness we see with our eyes. It is affected by distance.
- **Intrinsic brightness**: the amount of light that the star actually emits.
It is like a light bulb that looks dim when it is far away. Therefore, a star that looks bright in the night sky is not necessarily a nearby star or one that is intrinsically bright. Apparent brightness alone cannot tell us the distance or the intrinsic brightness.

The **color** of a star is related to its surface temperature. In general, bluish stars have high surface temperatures, and reddish stars are relatively cool. The Sun is close to yellow in color, and its surface temperature is about 5,500 degrees Celsius. This is similar to heated iron, which glows red and then, when it becomes even hotter, changes from white to blue.

Stars also have a life cycle. A star similar to the Sun roughly goes through the following stages. A cloud of gas and dust in space gathers under gravity to form a **protostar**. When nuclear fusion starts in its core, it shines steadily for a long time as a **main-sequence star**. When its fuel runs low, its outer layers swell greatly and it becomes a **red giant**, and finally a **white dwarf** remains, a small, hot core.

explain: Stars of much greater mass have shorter lives, and many of them end with a large explosion called a **supernova**. Many of the elements in our bodies and in the Earth, such as carbon and oxygen, were made inside stars and scattered into space in this way. The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and is currently in the main-sequence stage.

Judging by apparent brightness alone, the two may look similar. So the distances must be measured separately. This is why methods such as parallax, covered in Lesson 6, are needed.

astro-05.title: Galaxies and the Scale of the Universe
explain: The universe is so vast that it is hard to imagine with human senses, and kilometers are an inconvenient unit for measuring it. So astronomy uses the **light-year**. **A light-year is a unit of distance, not of time.** It is the distance light travels through a vacuum in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers. The speed of light is about 300,000 kilometers per second.

A light-year has another meaning. If a celestial object is 4 light-years away, the light we see from it now left about 4 years ago. Observing a distant object means seeing its **past appearance**. The nearest star other than the Sun is a little over 4 light-years away, and the Andromeda Galaxy, a relatively nearby large galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.

Stars do not float alone; they form large groups bound by gravity. A **galaxy** is a large collection of countless stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. The galaxy to which the Solar System belongs is the **Milky Way** (our galaxy), which is estimated to contain hundreds of billions of stars. Galaxies also gather under gravity to form **galaxy clusters**.

The scales from smallest to largest are as follows.
1. Earth
2. Solar System (the Sun and the celestial bodies that orbit it)
3. Milky Way (the galaxy that includes the Solar System)
4. Galaxy cluster (a collection of many galaxies)

So is this universe standing still? In the early 20th century, observations showed that light from distant galaxies is generally shifted toward the **red (longer-wavelength) side**, so it appears redder than it originally was. This is called **redshift**. How light is separated into colors is covered in Lesson 6. Redshift appears when a galaxy is moving away from us. Observations show that most distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This is an important observational piece of evidence for the **expansion of the universe**, in which the space between galaxies itself stretches. It is like points drawn on the surface of a balloon, all moving apart as the balloon is inflated. No single point is the center of the expansion.

Among stars in the same direction in the sky, the light from a nearby star left only a few years ago, while the light from a distant galaxy left millions of years ago. To look at the sky is to see many different pasts at once.

astro-06.title: How Astronomy Knows What It Knows
explain: Astronomers cannot go to stars and galaxies and touch them. Instead, they analyze the **light** that has come from them. In addition to visible light, they use light the eye cannot see, such as radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet and X-rays (electromagnetic waves). Different celestial objects emit different kinds of light, so gathering different kinds of light lets us learn much more. The instrument that gathers light is the **telescope**.

When light is spread out by color (wavelength), as a prism does, the result is called a **spectrum**. In a starlight spectrum, dark lines appear at certain places across the colored bands. This happens because gas in the star's outer layers absorbs light of particular colors, and each element produces lines at fixed positions. Therefore, the positions of the lines tell us which elements the star contains. If the spectral lines are shifted toward the red overall, that is a clue that the object is moving away from us. This is the redshift of Lesson 5.

explain.alt: A horizontal band runs from the blue end on the left toward the red end on the right, with colors in the sequence violet, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. Four thin vertical dark lines cross the band, each with a triangle below it pointing to the line. The title says it is an example of the shape of a spectrum that spreads starlight by color.
explain.caption: Dark lines in a spectrum (illustrative example showing the shape)

explain: The distance to a nearby star is measured by **parallax**. Hold a finger up in front of your eyes and close one eye at a time: the finger seems to shift position against the distant background. By the same principle, when Earth moves around the Sun to the opposite side of its orbit, a nearby star appears at a slightly different position against the distant background stars. The difference in position is measured as an angle, and the distance can be calculated from the properties of triangles. The larger the angle, the nearer the star.

explain.alt: Near the bottom is the Sun, and at both ends of the elliptical orbit around it are Earth ① and Earth ②. Lines from both Earths pass through a nearby star in the upper middle and extend up to the distant background stars above. Where each line reaches, there is an orange dot: from Earth ① the star appears to the right, and from Earth ② it appears to the left, so the nearby star appears to be in different places against the background.
explain.caption: Principle of parallax (schematic, not to scale)

explain: This method works only for nearby stars. A very distant star has a position difference that is too small to measure, so its distance must be found by other methods.

Finally, let us look at how science builds knowledge. What astronomers know consists of observed **evidence** and the **models** that explain it. The life cycle of a star and the structure of the Solar System are models, and models are tested against new observations and revised when necessary. Making no claim without evidence, and being willing to revise a model in the face of new evidence, is the method astronomy has built up over time.

astro-07.title: Annual Parallax and the Parsec: The First Rung of the Cosmic Distance Ladder
explain: One of the hardest problems in astronomy is **distance**. The stars in the sky appear to be attached to the same round ceiling, so a faint nearby star and a bright distant star cannot be told apart by appearance alone. Without distance, we cannot know a star's true brightness, size or mass. Astronomy therefore builds a **distance ladder**, measuring distances step by step, starting with the nearest objects.

The first rung is geometry. Because Earth orbits the Sun over the course of a year, observing the same star six months apart changes our line of sight slightly. A nearby star appears to shift its position a little against the far background stars. Half of this full angular shift is called the **annual parallax** $p$. It is a very thin, long triangle whose base is the radius of Earth's orbit (1 AU).

When the angle is very small, $\tan p \approx p$ (in radians), so the distance is $d = \frac{1\text{ AU}}{p}$. For convenience, astronomers defined a unit of distance for this purpose. The distance at which the annual parallax is 1 arcsecond (1″ = 1/3600°) is called **1 parsec (pc)**, which is about 3.26 light-years, or about $3.09 \times 10^{13}$ km. The formula then becomes very simple: $$d\text{(pc)} = \frac{1}{p\text{('')}}$$ A parallax of 0.5″ corresponds to 2 pc, and 0.1″ corresponds to 10 pc.

The nearest star other than the Sun, Proxima Centauri, has an annual parallax of about 0.77″, which corresponds to a distance of about 1.3 pc. Every star's parallax is smaller than 1″. Compared with the motions visible to the naked eye in the sky, this is an enormously small angle. For this reason, annual parallax was first measured only in the 19th century, when telescopes and precision measurement techniques had advanced. The fact that stars show such tiny parallaxes was itself evidence that stars are far more distant than people had imagined.

Limitation: As distance grows, the parallax becomes smaller, and measurement error takes up a larger share. Ground-based telescopes were limited to roughly tens to about 100 pc because of atmospheric turbulence, while space telescopes (such as Gaia) have extended this to thousands of pc or more. Beyond that, parallax cannot measure distance, so the ladder continues with the **brightness-based methods** of the next lesson. Upper rungs of the ladder depend on calibration from the lower rungs, so an error in the first rung propagates into the distances to the whole universe.

astro-08.title: Magnitudes and the Distance Modulus: Measuring Distance by Brightness
explain: How can we find the distance to a faraway star whose parallax cannot be measured? The principle is simple. A **light bulb of equal intrinsic brightness** looks dimmer the farther away it is. If we can determine a star's intrinsic brightness by some other method, we can compare it with the apparent brightness and find the distance. For this purpose, astronomy uses **magnitude**, a special brightness scale.

In ancient times, the brightest stars were called first magnitude, and stars barely visible to the naked eye were called sixth magnitude. In the 19th century, Pogson made this quantitative, so that **a difference of exactly 5 magnitudes corresponds to exactly 100 times the brightness**. A difference of 1 magnitude then corresponds to $100^{1/5} \approx 2.512$ times. The key points are that **smaller numbers mean brighter objects** and that the scale is logarithmic. $$m_1 - m_2 = -2.5\log_{10}\frac{F_1}{F_2}$$ $F$ is the amount of light we receive (radiant flux).

The brightness we observe is called the **apparent magnitude** $m$. To compare the intrinsic brightnesses of stars, all stars must be placed at the same distance. Taking 10 pc as that reference distance, the magnitude a star would have if placed at 10 pc is called its **absolute magnitude** $M$. Because light intensity falls off with the square of distance, the difference between the two magnitudes depends only on distance. $$m - M = 5\log_{10}d - 5 \quad (d\text{는 pc})$$ $m - M$ is called the **distance modulus**. At 10 pc it is 0, at 100 pc it is 5, and at 1000 pc it is 10.

A celestial object whose absolute magnitude can be determined independently is called a **standard candle**. A representative example is the **Cepheid variable star**. These stars vary in brightness with a fixed period, and the longer the period, the greater the absolute luminosity (the period–luminosity relation). By measuring the period, we know the absolute magnitude; comparing it with the apparent magnitude gives the distance. If the Cepheids nearby have their distances calibrated by parallax, then a Cepheid in a galaxy tens of millions of light-years away gives the distance to that galaxy.

Limitation: Starlight that passes through interstellar dust is dimmed, a phenomenon called **interstellar extinction**. If it is not corrected for, distances are overestimated. Also, if the absolute-magnitude calibration of a standard candle is wrong, every distance built on top of it is wrong too. Magnitudes depend on the wavelength band observed, so they must be compared within the same band.

Step 1: The difference is 5 magnitudes, so the brightness ratio is 100. Star A, with the smaller number, looks 100 times brighter.

astro-09.title: Blackbody Radiation: The Temperature and Size of Stars
explain: We cannot insert a thermometer into a star. However, from the **color** and **brightness** of starlight alone, we can find its surface temperature and even its size. The key to this is the law governing light emitted by hot objects, **blackbody radiation**.

An ideal object that absorbs all light is called a **blackbody**. The distribution of light emitted by a blackbody is determined by **temperature** alone. A star is not a perfect blackbody, but it is a fairly good approximation. As temperature rises, two things change. First, the wavelength of brightest emission becomes shorter (**Wien's displacement law**). Second, the total energy emitted per unit surface area increases sharply, in proportion to the fourth power of temperature (the Stefan–Boltzmann law, σT⁴). In symbols (original Korean wording kept around the formulas): $$\lambda_{max} = \frac{b}{T}, \quad b \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\cdot\text{K}$$ 둘째, 단위 표면적에서 나오는 총에너지가 온도의 네제곱에 비례해 급격히 커진다(**슈테판-볼츠만 법칙**): $\sigma T^4$.

Wien's law shows that color tells us the temperature. The Sun (about 5800 K) is brightest at $\lambda_{max} \approx 500$ nm, in the middle of the visible range (green to yellow). A star at 3000 K peaks at about 970 nm (infrared), so it looks red, while a star at 30000 K peaks at about 97 nm (ultraviolet), so it looks blue. A star's color is a thermometer for its surface.

**Luminosity**, the total energy a star emits, is the surface area multiplied by the emission per unit area. For a sphere of radius $R$, the relation is as follows. Knowing the luminosity and the temperature lets us find the radius. Luminosity comes from distance and apparent brightness (lessons 1–2), and temperature comes from color or spectrum. In solar units the relation is convenient (original Korean wording kept around the formulas): $$L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$$ 이다. 광도와 온도를 알면 반지름을 구할 수 있다. 광도는 거리와 겉보기 밝기에서(1~2교시), 온도는 색이나 스펙트럼에서 얻는다. 태양 단위로 쓰면 편리하다: $\frac{L}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2\left(\frac{T}{T_\odot}\right)^4$.

This relation is the key to understanding the H-R diagram of the next stage. If two stars have the same temperature but one is much more luminous, it must have the larger radius and is therefore a **giant**. If a star is hot but has low luminosity, its radius must be very small, so it is a **white dwarf**.

Limitation: The spectra of real stars contain **absorption lines**, where elements in the atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths, so they are not perfect blackbody curves. In fact, these absorption lines tell us the composition and temperature of a star more precisely (stage 3). Also, interstellar dust scatters blue light more strongly, making stars look redder than they are (interstellar reddening), so this must be corrected for when temperature is measured from color.

astro-10.title: Spectral Types and the H-R Diagram
explain: In the early 20th century, astronomers classifying the spectra of hundreds of thousands of stars discovered a remarkable order. When the temperatures and luminosities of stars are plotted on one graph, they do not scatter at random but cluster into a few groups. This graph is the **Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (H-R diagram)**, a map for understanding the life of stars.

The kinds and strengths of the **absorption lines** in a star's spectrum depend mainly on surface temperature. Based on this, stars are classified from hottest to coolest into the **O, B, A, F, G, K, M** spectral types. O-type stars, above 30,000 K, show lines of ionized helium; A-type stars, at about 10,000 K, have the strongest hydrogen lines; G-type stars (like the Sun), at about 6,000 K, show metal lines; and M-type stars, below 3,500 K, show molecular bands. The differences in absorption lines arise mainly from **differences in the state of atoms with temperature**, rather than from differences in composition.

explain.alt: H-R diagram. The horizontal axis is surface temperature (K), hot on the left, with tick marks at 30,000, 10,000, 6,000 and 3,000. The vertical axis is luminosity (Sun = 1), from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁶. A band running from the upper left to the lower right is labeled "main sequence." Star A is at about 20,000 K with luminosity 10⁴ (on the band); star B is at about 5,800 K with luminosity 1 (on the band); star C is at about 3,800 K with luminosity about 800 (upper right of the band); star D is at about 10,000 K with luminosity 10⁻³ (lower left of the band).

explain: The H-R diagram places surface temperature on the horizontal axis (hot on the left, spectral types running O→M) and luminosity on the vertical axis (brighter toward the top). About 90% of stars lie on the band running from the upper left to the lower right, the **main sequence**. Main-sequence stars are those that convert hydrogen into helium in their cores, and their position along the main sequence is determined mainly by their **mass**. More massive stars are hotter and brighter, so they lie toward the upper left.

There are also groups outside the main sequence. In the upper right are cool but very luminous **giants and supergiants**, and in the lower left are hot but very dim **white dwarfs**. As in the blackbody radiation of stage 2, $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$, so the position on the H-R diagram alone lets us compare radii. Moving toward the upper right means larger, and toward the lower left means smaller. On the H-R diagram, stars of equal radius lie along a diagonal straight line.

On the main sequence, a **mass–luminosity relation** holds. Roughly $L \propto M^{3.5}$, so a star with twice the mass has about 11 times the luminosity. Its fuel (mass) has doubled, but it burns that fuel 11 times faster, so **more massive stars have shorter lives**. The lifetime is roughly proportional to $M/L \propto M^{-2.5}$. If the main-sequence lifetime of the Sun is about 10 billion years, a star of 10 solar masses lasts only about 30 million years.

Limitation: A position on the H-R diagram is a snapshot taken at the time of observation; a single point does not describe a star's whole life. Also, determining luminosity requires distance, so errors in distance pass directly into errors on the vertical axis. The exponent 3.5 in the mass–luminosity relation is an average for the mass range near the Sun, and it differs for very light or very massive stars.

astro-11.title: Inside Stars: Hydrostatic Equilibrium and Nuclear Fusion
explain: The Sun has shone with nearly the same brightness for 4.6 billion years. What is the source of energy that lasts so long and so steadily, and why does a huge ball of gas neither collapse nor disperse? The interior of a star cannot be observed directly, but its structure can be reconstructed from physical laws.

The force that holds a star together is its own **gravity**, and the force that keeps it from collapsing is the **pressure** of its internal gas. In each layer, the pressure from below pushes upward with a force that balances the weight of the layers above. This is **hydrostatic equilibrium**, $\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{GM(r)\rho}{r^2}$, the same balance we met for the atmosphere in Earth science. Pressure and temperature rise toward the center of a star; the center of the Sun reaches about 15 million K.

The energy source is **nuclear fusion**. At the high temperature of the core, hydrogen nuclei (protons) overcome their electrical repulsion and fuse. In stars like the Sun, the **proton–proton chain** converts four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus. A helium nucleus is about **0.7%** lighter than the four protons that make it up. This mass difference is released as energy according to $E = mc^2$ (physics stage 5). In more massive stars, the CNO cycle, which uses carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as catalysts, is the main pathway.

The Sun converts about 4 million tons of mass into energy every second. That may sound enormous, but compared with the Sun's mass it is extremely small; even using only part of the hydrogen in the core, it can shine for about 10 billion years. If it were chemical burning, it would last only a few thousand years. This is why the age of the Sun was a mystery until the end of the 19th century, and nuclear physics solved it.

Hydrostatic equilibrium and nuclear fusion regulate each other. If fusion speeds up slightly, the core heats up and its pressure rises, so the core expands and cools, which slows the reaction again. Conversely, if the reaction slows, the core contracts and heats up, which speeds it up again. Thanks to this **negative feedback**, main-sequence stars shine steadily for a long time. The energy produced in the core is carried to the surface over tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of years: by radiation in the inner layers and by convection in the outer layers.

Limitation: This lesson simplifies the star as a spherically symmetric, static object. Real stars rotate, have magnetic fields, and lose matter from their outer layers. The only nearly direct way to confirm fusion in the core is to detect the neutrinos that escape directly from the center.

astro-12.title: Stellar Evolution and Death by Mass
explain: Stars are born and they die. And one number almost entirely determines a star's life: its **mass** at birth. Depending on mass, a star may become a white dwarf that slowly cools, or it may leave behind a neutron star or a black hole in one of the most violent explosions in the universe.

**After the main sequence**: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the helium core contracts and heats up, while hydrogen fusion continues in a shell around it. The outer layers of the star swell greatly and the surface cools, and the star becomes a **red giant**. On the H-R diagram it moves away from the main sequence toward the upper right. When the core reaches about 100 million K, helium begins to fuse into carbon and oxygen.

**Stars of roughly solar mass (about 8 solar masses or less)**: They never become hot enough to fuse the carbon–oxygen core further. The outer layers gradually disperse into space to form a beautiful **planetary nebula**, and the hot core that remains becomes a **white dwarf**. A white dwarf is an object with about the mass of the Sun packed into the size of the Earth. With no fusion, it is held up by **electron degeneracy pressure** (a quantum-mechanical pressure), and it cools slowly. The largest mass that electron degeneracy pressure can support is about 1.4 solar masses (the Chandrasekhar limit).

**Massive stars (about 8 solar masses or more)**: The core burns carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon in turn, building an onion-like layered structure, until it reaches **iron**. Iron is the most stable atomic nucleus, so fusing iron does not release energy; it requires energy. The core, its fuel exhausted, collapses in an instant, and a **supernova explosion** blows away the outer layers. The remaining core becomes a **neutron star** (about 20 km in diameter, held up by neutron degeneracy pressure) or, if it is more massive, no pressure can withstand gravity and it becomes a **black hole**.

The death of stars makes the materials of the universe. Fusion inside stars and supernova explosions produce carbon, oxygen, iron and even heavier elements, which spread through the universe. This matter becomes the raw material for the next generation of stars, planets and life. Most of the carbon and oxygen in our bodies were made inside stars of the past.

Limitation: The mass boundaries (such as about 8 solar masses) are approximate and depend on the star's composition (metal content), rotation and mass loss. In particular, a star in a **binary** may exchange matter with its companion and follow a path entirely different from that of a single star. If a white dwarf that receives matter from its companion exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit, a different type of supernova (Type Ia) occurs.

astro-13.title: Kepler's Laws and Measuring the Mass of Celestial Bodies
explain: The mass of a planet or star cannot be weighed on a scale. However, by observing how another celestial body orbits it, we can determine its mass. The tools for this are Kepler's laws of planetary motion, and their generalization by Newton in the form of gravity.

**Kepler's three laws**: ① Planets orbit the Sun along **ellipses** with the Sun at one focus. ② The line connecting a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times (**constant areal velocity**). Therefore a planet moves fast when it is close to the Sun and slowly when it is far away. This is a consequence of conservation of angular momentum. ③ The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of the orbit ($P^2 \propto a^3$). In the Solar System, when $P$ is in years and $a$ is in AU, $P^2 = a^3$.

Newton showed that Kepler's third law follows from universal gravitation, and in the process found that the proportionality constant contains **mass**. If the mass of the orbiting body (m) is much smaller than that of the central body (M), then M + m ≈ M. So measuring a satellite's orbital period and radius gives the mass of the central body. In units of solar masses, AU and years, the law becomes very simple, M + m = a³/P². In symbols (original Korean wording kept around the formulas): $$P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G(M + m)}a^3$$ 주위를 도는 천체의 질량 $m$이 중심 천체 $M$보다 훨씬 작으면 $M + m \approx M$이다. 즉 **위성의 궤도 주기와 반지름을 재면 중심 천체의 질량을 알 수 있다**. 태양 질량 단위·AU·년을 쓰면 $M + m = a^3/P^2$으로 아주 간단해진다.

With this method, the masses of planets in the Solar System are measured from the orbits of their moons, and the masses of stars are measured from the orbits of **binary stars** (two stars orbiting each other). In a binary, the two stars orbit a common center of mass, so the ratio of their distances from that center is inversely proportional to their mass ratio ($m_1 a_1 = m_2 a_2$). Stellar masses measured this way provided the basis for the mass–luminosity relation of stage 3. The mass of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way (about 4 million solar masses) was also measured from the orbits of the stars around it.

In an elliptical orbit, the speed varies with position. The circular-orbit speed is $v = \sqrt{GM/a}$ (physics stage 2), and in an ellipse the speed is greatest at periapsis (closest point) and smallest at apoapsis (farthest point). According to constant areal velocity, (speed at periapsis) × (distance at periapsis) = (speed at apoapsis) × (distance at apoapsis).

Limitation: This method assumes that only two bodies exert gravity on each other. When several bodies pull on one another, the orbits change slightly (perturbation). The existence of Neptune was predicted from perturbations of Uranus's orbit. Also, if the orbital plane of a binary is tilted relative to our line of sight, the inclination must be known separately to find the true size of the orbit.

astro-14.title: Escape Velocity and the Virial Theorem
explain: How fast must a rocket go to escape Earth forever? Why do the galaxies in a galaxy cluster stay bound together instead of flying apart? Both questions can be answered by comparing **kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy**.

The gravitational potential energy of an object at the surface of a body of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is $-\frac{GMm}{R}$ (zero at infinite distance). For the object to travel infinitely far away, its kinetic energy must cancel this negative potential energy, so $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{R}$, and the **escape velocity** does not depend on the object's mass. For Earth it is about 11.2 km/s, and for the Moon about 2.4 km/s; it is √2 times the circular orbital speed. In symbols (original Korean wording kept around the formulas): $$v_{esc} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}$$ 이다. 물체의 질량 $m$과 무관하다. 지구는 약 11.2 km/s, 달은 약 2.4 km/s다. 원 궤도 속력 $\sqrt{GM/R}$의 $\sqrt{2}$배다.

Consider the radius at which the escape velocity reaches the speed of light. From $c = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, we get $R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$. This is the **Schwarzschild radius**. If a mass is compressed inside it, even light cannot escape, and it becomes a black hole. For the mass of the Sun, it is about 3 km. (An exact derivation requires general relativity, but the same formula results.)

When several bodies are bound together by gravity and form a system that stays stable for a long time, between the time-averaged kinetic energy $K$ and the potential energy $U$, the **virial theorem** $2K + U = 0$ holds. For a single circular orbit, $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$, so exactly $2K = -U$.

The virial theorem becomes a tool for measuring **invisible mass**. Measuring the velocity dispersion (the spread of speeds) of the galaxies in a galaxy cluster gives $K$; the virial theorem then gives $U$, and therefore the total mass. In the 1930s, Zwicky used this method on the Coma galaxy cluster and found a mass hundreds of times larger than that of the visible stars. The galaxies were moving so fast that they should have dispersed unless there was invisible mass holding them together. This is one of the first pieces of evidence for **dark matter** (continued in stage 5).

Limitation: The virial theorem holds only when the system is in **equilibrium**. Applying it to a system that has not reached equilibrium, such as a galaxy cluster that is currently colliding, gives the wrong mass. Also, the velocity dispersion can measure only the line-of-sight component, so the method requires the assumption that the motions are distributed evenly in all directions.

astro-15.title: Exoplanet Search: Transits and Radial Velocity
explain: **Exoplanets**, planets that orbit other stars, were first clearly detected in the 1990s, and thousands are now known. However, planets are billions of times fainter than their stars, so most of them cannot be seen directly. Astronomers look for planets by measuring **small changes that appear in the star**. The two main methods are the transit method and the radial velocity method.

**Transit method**: When a planet's orbital plane is nearly aligned with our line of sight, the planet passes in front of its star, and each time it does, the starlight is slightly blocked and the star dims. The fractional dimming is the ratio of the areas of the planet's disk and the star's disk: $$\frac{\Delta F}{F} = \left(\frac{R_p}{R_\star}\right)^2$$ Therefore, the depth of the dimming gives the **radius of the planet**, and the interval between repeated dimmings gives the **orbital period**. When Jupiter crosses a Sun-sized star, the star dims by about 1%; Earth dims it by about 0.008%.

explain.alt: The horizontal axis is time (days, 0 to 10) and the vertical axis is relative brightness. The brightness stays at 1.000 for most of the time, with two identical dips to 0.990, one at day 3 and one at day 7, each lasting briefly before returning to 1.000.

explain: **Radial velocity method**: A planet and its star orbit a common center of mass. So the star also moves in a tiny circle, alternately approaching and receding from us. As it approaches, its spectral lines shift slightly toward the blue, and as it recedes, toward the red (**Doppler effect**). From the period and size of this wobble, the **mass of the planet** is obtained (more precisely, a minimum mass that depends on the inclination of the orbit). A massive planet that orbits close to its star causes a larger wobble. Jupiter makes the Sun wobble by about 13 m/s; Earth makes it wobble by about 0.09 m/s.

Using both methods together is powerful. Knowing the radius from the transit and the mass from the radial velocity gives the **average density**, which lets us judge whether a planet is rocky or gaseous. During a transit, the starlight that passes through the planet's atmosphere creates absorption lines, and analyzing them can even reveal the composition of the atmosphere.

Limitations and biases: Transits occur only for the small fraction of planets whose orbits are nearly aligned with our line of sight. Both methods find **large, massive planets close to their stars** more easily, so the list of discovered planets does not directly represent the true distribution (an observational selection effect). Starspots or pulsations can look like planetary signals, so repeated observations and confirmation by other methods are needed.

astro-16.title: Galactic Rotation Curves and Dark Matter
explain: A spiral galaxy like our own Milky Way is a giant disk in which hundreds of billions of stars revolve around its center. The **rotation curve** shows how fast the stars orbit at each distance from the center. The rotation curve precisely measured in the 1970s by Vera Rubin and others was entirely different from what was expected, and it became one of the strongest pieces of evidence for **dark matter**.

The circular orbital speed is determined by the mass inside the orbit: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM(r)}{r}}$ (stage 4). In a spiral galaxy, the stars and gas are concentrated in the center and become rapidly sparser outward. Therefore, beyond the radius that encloses nearly all the visible matter, $M(r)$ hardly increases, so the speed should **decline** as $v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$, as it does for the planets of the Solar System (Keplerian decline).

explain.alt: The horizontal axis is distance from the galaxy's center (kpc, 0 to 30) and the vertical axis is rotation speed (km/s, 0 to 300). The solid line of observed values rises rapidly from the center and then stays almost constant at about 220 km/s beyond about 5 kpc. The dashed line, labeled "expected from visible matter alone," matches the observed values up to about 5 kpc, then gradually decreases to about 80 km/s at 30 kpc.

explain: However, the observed rotation curve is **almost flat** even at the outer radii, as the figure shows. For $v$ to stay constant, $M(r) = v^2r/G$, that is, the mass must **keep increasing in proportion to the radius**. The conclusion is that a substance that emits little light but reveals itself through its gravity must surround the galaxy in a rounded halo. This **dark matter halo** has a mass several to more than ten times that of the visible matter.

Independent evidence points in the same direction: the virial mass of galaxy clusters (stage 4), the mass measured by **gravitational lensing**, in which a massive object bends the light from objects behind it, the analysis of the cosmic microwave background in the final lesson of stage 5, and observations of colliding galaxy clusters (such as the Bullet Cluster), in which the distribution of visible matter and the distribution of mass do not match. In the current standard cosmology, dark matter makes up about 85% of all the matter in the universe.

However, we **do not know what dark matter is**. It is presumed to be an unknown particle that interacts little with light, but it has not yet been detected directly, either in underground detection experiments or in accelerator experiments. Another possibility being studied is **modified gravity**, in which the law of gravity itself changes at very weak accelerations. These theories explain the rotation curves of individual galaxies well, but they have difficulty explaining other evidence, such as galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background, all together. Science keeps the 'observed phenomenon' and its 'interpretation' distinct.

astro-17.title: The Hubble–Lemaître Law and Cosmic Expansion
explain: In the 1920s, astronomers measuring the spectra of distant galaxies found that the light of nearly every galaxy was shifted toward the **red**. Moreover, the farther the galaxy, the larger the shift. This simple observation led to the most important discovery of the 20th century: the universe is expanding.

When a spectral line shifts from its original wavelength $\lambda_0$ to $\lambda$, the **redshift** is $z = \frac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}$. For nearby galaxies ($z \ll 1$), this is interpreted as the Doppler effect, giving a recession velocity $v \approx cz$. Lemaître and Hubble showed that the distances of galaxies (measured with Cepheid variables and other methods from stage 2) are **proportional** to their recession velocities. $$v = H_0 d$$ 비례 상수 $H_0$ (the proportionality constant) is the **Hubble constant**, currently about 70 km/s/Mpc. For every 1 Mpc of distance, the recession velocity increases by about 70 km/s.

explain.alt: The horizontal axis is distance (Mpc, 0 to 200) and the vertical axis is recession velocity (km/s, 0 to 15,000). Points representing galaxies are scattered near a dashed straight line that passes through the origin, and one point at (100, 7000) is marked.

explain: This relation does not mean that we are at the center of the universe. As a raisin bread rises, from any raisin the other raisins move away, and the farther ones move faster. When space itself expands uniformly, **the same law holds from any galaxy**. The cosmological redshift is understood not as galaxies racing through space, but as the result of **space stretching and thereby lengthening the wavelength** while light travels.

If we run the expansion backward, everything was closer together in the past. If the expansion had proceeded at a constant rate, the time for a galaxy now at distance $d$ to reach its present position would be $d/v = 1/H_0$. This **Hubble time** is about 14 billion years when $H_0 = 70$. The actual expansion rate has changed over time (first decelerating and then accelerating), but this value is similar in scale to the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years).

Limitation: $v = cz$ is an approximation that holds when $z$ is small. When $z$ approaches 1, expressions that include relativistic effects and the history of the expansion must be used. Also, for nearby galaxies, the **peculiar motion** caused by gravity can be larger than the expansion velocity; the Andromeda Galaxy, for example, is actually approaching us. The exact value of the Hubble constant differs by a few percent depending on the measurement method, and this discrepancy is an actively studied problem today.

astro-18.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background and Critical Density
explain: If the universe is expanding, the early universe must have been smaller, hotter and denser. Might the light from that hot era still survive somewhere? The faint radio noise that comes from the whole sky, discovered by chance in 1965, was exactly that light: the **cosmic microwave background (CMB)**.

The early universe was a hot plasma, so light kept colliding with free electrons and could not travel straight. When expansion cooled the universe to about 3000 K (about 380,000 years after the Big Bang), electrons combined with nuclei to form neutral atoms, and light began to travel freely. Since then, as the universe has expanded by about 1100 times, the wavelength of that light has stretched, so it is now observed as blackbody radiation with a temperature of **about 2.7 K**. By Wien's law (stage 2), $\lambda_{max} \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-3}/2.7 \approx 1.1$ mm, which is microwave.

The CMB is a **nearly perfect blackbody spectrum** and has nearly the same temperature in every direction of the sky. This is strong evidence for the Big Bang model, which holds that the early universe was hot and uniform. However, examined precisely, it contains tiny **temperature fluctuations** at the level of one part in 100,000. These fluctuations were small differences in density at that time, which grew under gravity to become the galaxies and galaxy clusters we see today. Analyzing the size distribution of the fluctuations allows us to determine the composition and geometry of the universe precisely.

The fate and geometry of the universe are determined by its density. The boundary density at which gravity could halt the expansion is called the **critical density**. With H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc it is about 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³, equivalent to about 5 to 6 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter. The ratio of the actual density to the critical density is the density parameter Ω. CMB analyses give Ω ≈ 1, that is, space is nearly flat. In symbols (original Korean wording kept around the formulas): $$\rho_c = \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}$$ 라 한다. $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc이면 약 $9 \times 10^{-27}$ kg/m³, 1 m³에 수소 원자 약 5~6개다. 실제 밀도와 임계밀도의 비를 **밀도 매개변수** $\Omega$라 한다. CMB 분석 결과 우주는 $\Omega \approx 1$, 즉 공간이 거의 **평탄**하다.

The composition is surprising. Of the present energy density of the universe, the ordinary matter (atoms) we know makes up about **5%**, dark matter about **27%**, and the remaining about **68%** is a mysterious **dark energy** that **accelerates** the expansion of the universe. Dark energy was first revealed in the late 1990s by observations showing that distant Type Ia supernovae (stage 3) are dimmer than expected. That 95% of the universe consists of components whose nature is unknown is the present state of modern cosmology.

Limitation: These figures are results from fitting many observations under the assumption of the standard cosmological model (ΛCDM). If the model itself is wrong, the interpretations change too. There are observations that reveal cracks in the model, such as the discrepancy in measurements of the Hubble constant, so cosmology remains a field that is being actively tested.

Since then the universe has expanded about 1100 times, and the wavelength of that light has stretched by the same factor through redshift. As a result, it is now blackbody radiation of about 2.7 K, and according to Wien's law it is brightest in the microwave region, near a wavelength of 1 mm.

astro-19.title: Capstone: Inferring the Physical Quantities of a Stellar System
explain: The first capstone lesson starts from observational data on a hypothetical stellar system and, step by step, uses the tools of stages 2 to 5 in turn to **work backward step by step to find the physical quantities of stars and planets**. This is the same way real observational astronomy proceeds. Because the result of each step becomes the input of the next, we also see how errors propagate.

**Observational data**: annual parallax 0.02″; apparent magnitude 6.0; the wavelength at which the spectrum's radiation is strongest, 500 nm; a light curve that dims by 0.5% every 3 days; and radial velocity oscillations with the same 3-day period.

**Step 1 (distance)**: $d = 1/0.02 = 50$ pc. **Step 2 (absolute magnitude)**: the distance modulus is $5\log 50 - 5 \approx 3.5$, so $M = 6.0 - 3.5 = 2.5$. Since the Sun's absolute magnitude is about 4.8, this star is about 2.3 magnitudes brighter, and its luminosity is $2.512^{2.3} \approx 8$ times the Sun's. **Step 3 (temperature)**: $T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}/5 \times 10^{-7} = 5800$ K, the same as the Sun's temperature.

**Step 4 (radius)**: Since the temperature equals the Sun's but the luminosity is 8 times larger, $(R/R_\odot)^2 = 8$, so $R \approx 2.8R_\odot$. This could be a star somewhat larger than a main-sequence star, one that is beginning to leave the main sequence. **Step 5 (planet)**: With a 0.5% dip, $R_p/R_\star = \sqrt{0.005} \approx 0.071$, so $R_p \approx 0.071 \times 2.8 \times 109 \approx 22$ Earth radii, about twice the size of Jupiter. The transits and radial velocity showing the same period strengthen the interpretation that they are signals from the same object.

**Error propagation and critique**: With an annual parallax of 0.02″ and an error of ±0.002″, the distance has an error of ±10%, the distance modulus ±0.2 magnitude, the luminosity ±20%, the star's radius ±10%, and the planet's radius ±10%. An error in the first rung of the distance ladder spreads to every result. In addition, we have ignored interstellar extinction and approximated the star as a blackbody. If the planet's radius is really this large, it could be a giant gaseous planet puffed up by heating close to its star, or it may not be a planet at all but a faint companion star; therefore its mass must be checked using the size of the radial velocity signal.

examples.title: Recomputing the luminosity
body: Given: absolute magnitude 2.5, and the Sun's 4.8.
Step 1: The magnitude difference is 2.3. The brightness ratio is $10^{0.4 \times 2.3} = 10^{0.92} \approx 8.3$.
Step 2: $2.512^{2.3}$ gives the same value, because $2.512 = 10^{0.4}$.

examples.title: Additional observations that could change the judgment
body: Observation A: The radial velocity wobble is very large, several km/s. The companion then has a large mass, so it is more likely a low-mass star (a binary) than a planet.

Observation B: A wobble of tens of m/s points to a planet with a mass on the order of Jupiter's. Compute its density together with its radius (22 Earth radii) to decide whether it is a puffed-up hot Jupiter.

astro-20.title: Capstone: Designing an Observation Plan and Critiquing the Interpretation
explain: The final task is to **choose one astronomical question, design an observation plan to answer it, and critique the interpretation and limits of the expected results**. Examples: "Is there a planet with a habitable temperature around this star?" "Does this galaxy also have a dark matter halo?" "How old is this star cluster?"

Framework for an observation plan: ① **Question**: convert it into physical quantities that can be measured. ② **Required observations**: which of position (parallax), brightness (photometry), spectrum (spectroscopy), and changes over time (light curves, radial velocity) are needed. ③ **Observing conditions**: the wavelength band (visible, infrared, radio), the precision, and the observing period (for example, how long one must observe to see two or more orbital periods). ④ **Analysis chain**: which laws take us from the observed quantities to the physical quantities. ⑤ **Uncertainties**: which errors enter where, and how they propagate.

Points to be especially careful about in astronomical interpretation: **selection effects** (bright and large objects are seen first), **propagation of errors in the distance ladder**, **projection along the line of sight** (orbital inclination; radial velocity gives only one component), and **model dependence** (blackbody approximations, standard cosmology). In addition, the **agreement of several independent methods** strengthens a conclusion more than any single observation.
This task is not graded. The text you submit is saved only on this device and can be viewed again under 'My notes' in 'My progress.'

examples.title: Sample plan: finding a planet in the habitable zone
body: Question: Is there a rocky planet in the habitable zone of star S (the range of distances where liquid water can exist)?

Observation and analysis: parallax gives the distance → luminosity → the orbital distance at which the stellar flux received is similar to Earth's → the orbital period at that distance (Kepler's third law) → a search for transits at that period (radius) plus radial velocity (mass) → a judgment of rockiness from the density.
Observing period: if the period is near one year, at least two or three transits must be observed, which requires 2–3 years or more.

Critique: The transit dip of an Earth-sized planet is only about 0.01%, which is hard to tell apart from variations due to starspots. The habitable zone depends on the planet's atmosphere, so it is only a "possibility."

examples.title: Sample plan: the age of a star cluster
body: Observation: photometry of the colors (temperatures) and brightnesses of the cluster's stars to draw an H-R diagram. All the stars are at the same distance, so their apparent magnitudes can be compared directly.
Analysis: read the mass at the point where the most massive stars on the main sequence have already left it (the turnoff point), and estimate the age from the main-sequence lifetime of that mass.
Critique: Interstellar extinction and the metal content of the cluster change star colors and evolutionary models, so both must be corrected for together.

checks.prompt: Choose your own astronomical question, and summarize in three to five sentences the observations and the chain of analysis it requires.
checks.hint: As in the sample plan, write question → observation → analysis → error.
checks.explanation: An observation plan needs a clear chain that leads to the conclusion.
checks.model: The question is: what are the masses of the two stars in the nearby binary X? First, measure the distance with annual parallax, and observe the orbit of the two stars on the sky with a telescope over several years to obtain the true semi-major axis and period. Measure the radial velocities of the two stars with spectroscopy to confirm the ratio of their distances from the center of mass. Use Kepler's third law to obtain the sum of the masses, and the distance ratio to obtain each star's mass. The orbital inclination and the parallax error are the main sources of error in the mass.
